title: Making the UNFCCC fit for purpose: A research agenda on vested interests and green spiralling

blocks: Received: 22 December 2023 | Revised: 5 February 2024 | Accepted: 14 February 2024
POLICYINSIGHTS
Making the UNFCCC fit for purpose: A research agenda on vested interests and green spiralling
Naghmeh Nasiritousi1,2 | Alexandra Buylova1 | Mathias Fridahl2 | Gunilla Reischl1
1Swedish Institute of International Affairs, Stockholm, Sweden

Abstract How can the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) be made more effective? This paper argues that in order to make the UNFCCC fit for purpose, there is a need to identify the specific institutional reforms that can create ripple effects to accelerate climate action across governance levels and relevant organisations. Longstanding calls to reform the UNFCCC have targeted inefficient procedures with the intent to promote effective outcomes and – after entry into force of the Paris Agreement – to transform the UNFCCC towards holding more implementation-­focused deliberations. Despite such calls, UNFCCC reform has been modest, at best. Central to the failure of reform proposals are vested interests with conflicts of interest that seek to obstruct climate action. Without addressing these elephants in the room, reform proposals will make modest contributions to overcoming key challenges. It is due time to start retargeting institutional reform from addressing procedural inefficiencies at the UNFCCC towards addressing vested interests. We propose a new research agenda to understand ways to undermine incumbent actors seeking to preserve business as usual and support new entrants that facilitate climate action through green spiralling. A reform process addressing vested interests could improve both procedural efficiency and implementation.

1 | IDENTIFYING THE NEED FOR UNFCCC REFORM

The latest round of climate negotiations in Dubai (COP 28) concluded the first global stocktake of the Paris Agreement. Negotiations aimed at a ‘course correction’ to set the world on a path to achieving the Paris Agreement goals. For the first time ever, nearly 200 countries agreed to ‘transition away from fossil fuels’ and ramp up clean energy in order to mitigate climate change (UNFCCC, 2023). While the outcome has been described as ‘historic’ by some, others viewed it as a ‘stab in the back for those most vulnerable’ (Filks et al., 2023, p. 1). Most observers have also commented on the fact that it took nearly three decades of climate negotiations to include language on fossil fuels, which clearly illustrates how difficult negotiations in this forum can be. While the real test for climate action will be the new rounds of Nationally Determined Contributions due in 2025, calls for reforming the UNFCCC are pro-liferating (see e.g., Rajamani et al., 2023; Rockström et al., 2023).

Here, we argue that discussions about various reform proposals need to put the purpose of reforms at the centre of analysis. Without an analysis of the root of the problem and an assessment of the possible effects of proposed solutions, there is a risk that the target of reform will miss the key challenges that need to be addressed and thereby tinker on the margins. By considering the context of reforms, we gain deeper insights into what the underlying issues are that need to be addressed. This is particularly important at a time

when the multilateral system is under stress and efforts are underway to reinvigorate multilateral institutions (UN, 2024).

While various multilateral institutions will face different needs for reform depending on their key challenges (see e.g., Kruck & Zangl, 2020; Weiss, 2011), the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) serves as an example that holds valuable lessons for other institutions, particularly in the environmental field. Despite progress with joint rules ratified by 195 Parties, countries are still not on track to fulfil the goals stated in the Paris Agreement (IPCC, 2023). While the UNFCCC is just one of several institutions in the climate governance landscape, many argue that the UNFCCC needs reforms to raise ambition and drive implementation (Rockström et al., 2023). These calls tend to aim at increasing procedural efficiency, ensuring greater transparency and accountability of pledges and initiatives, streamlining agendas, and managing the size of the UNFCCC's Annual Conference of the Parties (COP) (Frey & Burgess, 2022; Rajamani et al., 2023). Others, such as Al Gore (see e.g., Borenstein & Keaten, 2023), argue that the consensus principle for decision-­making is holding progress back and that this should be the target for reform (also see e.g., Kemp, 2016).

In this policy insights article, we argue that such proposals will do little to advance progress and instead highlight that reforms need to address an issue that is at the heart of slow progress on climate change, namely vested interests aiming to preserve the status quo. Vested interests are here defined as actors who have a special interest in existing systems and seek to exert controlling influence on those systems (Vormedal et al., 2023). Vested interests that act to stop or weaken climate legislation have been identified at all levels of governance, from the state level to the international level (Kinley et al., 2021; Meckling & Nahm, 2022; Mildenberger, 2020; Stoddard et al., 2021). Although the mechanisms behind slow progress in the UNFCCC are multi-­faceted and complex, the unbalanced influence of vested interests seeking to preserve the status quo compared to interests invested in promoting climate-­resilient and low-­carbon development path-ways deserves more attention. To overcome problems inherent to multilateral climate cooperation and accelerate progress on climate action, we argue that reforms should target the role of vested interests that engage in obstruction of climate action.

Our argument is in line with recent research that conceptualizes climate change as a problem of existential politics, whereby different interests ‘not only fight over who gets what but also over whose way of life survives’ (Colgan et al., 2021, p. 592). As such, a core challenge facing climate governance is that influential actors with strong vested interests in maintaining business as usual are unlikely to accept reforms that undermine their influence. Some literature has begun examining how to weaken obstructionist vested interests (Meckling & Nahm, 2022). With this article, we harness different strands of research to open a research agenda on how reforms could be designed to challenge vested interests and how to set off a ‘green spiral’ (Kelsey, 2021) whereby actors who support climate action are strengthened. In doing so, we highlight the potentials and challenges of institutional reform aimed at strengthening climate progress.
2 | THE PARIS AGREEMENT: A WATERSHED FOR UNFCCC REFORM CALLS

Since the adoption of the UNFCCC in 1992, the Convention has played a central role in global climate governance. Over the past decades, countries have clashed over many issues centred around key questions of transparency and responsibility for climate change. The process has recurringly been described as ‘painstakingly slow’ (Andresen, 2015, p. 15; Eckersley, 2012, p. 35; Falkner et al., 2010, p. 258). At the root of slow progress lies the Convention's provision that Parties must ‘agree upon and adopt, by consensus, rules of procedure’ (UNFCCC, 1992, Article 7.2 k). The consensus requirement has continuously blocked agreement on voting procedures and the COPs have had to revert to the provisional application of draft rules exempting the possibility to vote. This, in effect, grants veto power to all Parties, and a tendency to search for least common denominators for agreements.

Despite these limitations, the UNFCCC has pro-duced two treaties under the Convention—the 1997 Kyoto Protocol and the 2015 Paris Agreement—that have shaped the global response to climate change. Calls for reform of the UNFCCC have, however, been continuous, although they have shifted in substance in the post-­Paris era. In the early period of negotiating the Kyoto Protocol and its rulebook, there was a heated debate centred on the slow progress (Michaelowa & Tol, 2002). Around the late 2000s and early 2010s, several researchers commented on the negotiations delivering far from sufficient results (see e.g., Vihma, 2014; Yamin & Depledge, 2010). Depledge (2006, p. 11) lamented that the consensus requirement for ‘even the most trivial and technical’ decisions ‘renders the climate change process painfully slow’. Many of these early reform calls aimed at making the UN climate negotiations more effective through more efficient procedures. A central underpinning logic of this critique was that the pace of climate change had outrun the diplomats. With the escalating climate crisis, it was argued, the UNFCCC must also step up.

The calls for UNFCCC reform targeting the inefficient process prevailed until the adoption of the Paris Agreement. The Agreement was hailed as a milestone for global climate governance, although its effectiveness has been questioned. Hale (2020, p. 86) describes it as ‘a positive but ultimately modest step.’ Reform proposals have somewhat shifted focus in the post-­Paris era. While the pre-­Paris calls for reform mostly targeted decision-­making procedures, the post-­ Paris reform proposals call for a change in the focus of the work of the UNFCCC. Bauer et al. (2020, p. 4) support to shift gears ‘from negotiations and rule-­setting to implementation’, Roesch and Curtin (2022) call for ‘transforming the UNFCCC into a platform that is more action-­oriented and focused on collectively addressing the climate emergency’, and Rockström et al. (2023) maintain that ‘all efforts must now be focused on one thing, delivery to enable a safe climate landing for humanity on Earth.’ Underlying these calls is the premise that the Paris Agreement provides all the necessary tools for climate action and, therefore, that ‘diplomatic needs are waning’ (Carlton & Victor, 2022).

We contend that it is premature to downplay the role of the UNFCCC in driving politically negotiated outcomes and that both the pre-­ and post-­Paris reformists have aimed at the wrong target. The vested interests of incumbent actors explain both why the UNFCCC makes slow progress and why the collective ambition in mid-­term climate action falls far short of what is necessary to achieve the long-­term goal (Kornek et al., 2020). More efficient procedures or a stronger focus on implementation will not change the root cause of inaction: namely, the vested interest of incumbent actors at influential positions in the current global sociotechnical regime.

To understand why this is the case, it is important to understand the key form and function of the UNFCCC and what can reasonably be expected of the multilateral process. The UNFCCC has limited enforcement tools and therefore the consensus principle ensures that outcomes are viewed as legitimate by all (Buylova et al., 2023; Vihma, 2015). The main functions of the UNFCCC include setting a minimum standard for countries to follow, sending political signals, developing norms for climate action, as well as facilitating capacity building, experience sharing, transparency, accountability, and encouraging coalitions of the willing. What is holding action back is therefore not so much lack of voting rules or little focus on implementation at the UNFCCC, but rather the strong position of vested interests, which underlie all processes. Specifically, concentrated economic interests that seek to preserve the status quo hold back climate action both through influencing weak outcomes at the UNFCCC and through blocking or weakening implementation of climate action at the domestic level (Nasiritousi, 2017; Stoddard et al., 2021; Zacher, 2023). In other words, unless the role of vested interests is addressed in reform proposals, other reform efforts will make little progress on making the UNFCCC fit for purpose.

Specifically, incumbent actors in the global energy system ‘hold a position of status and power in relation to markets and institutions’ (Altunay & Bergek, 2023, p. 5), which combined with applying draft rules of procedure for the negotiations provides ‘nation states with rich fossil fuel resources’ a ‘disproportionate influence on international policymaking’ (Lucas, 2021, p. 2). The difficulty with making progress on UNFCCC reform is thus how to convince incumbent actors to support reforms that would reduce their influence.
3 | THE ROLE OF VESTED INTERESTS

Typically, actors with vested interests in the climate context have been depicted as incumbent actors who resist change and promote business as usual (Boon, 2019). These include the fossil fuel industry and other powerful business interests that rely on the use of fossil fuels (Stoddard et al., 2021). Such vested interests exert undue influence on climate policymaking by blocking or watering down climate policies at different levels of governance (Grasso, 2019; Moe, 2015; Newell & Paterson, 1998). This often takes place through political lobbying, greenwashing and by funding disinformation campaigns (Nasiritousi, 2017; Stoddard et al., 2021; Zacher, 2023). Such vested interests ‘have strong incentives to act as gatekeepers of policy institutions enabling the continuation of fossil-­ fuel-­based industrial practices’ (Vormedal et al., 2023, p. 1). However, vested interests also include groups of actors that want to promote change. These include new entrants and green businesses that have an interest in expanding markets for green products that target emissions reductions (Moe, 2015). Thus, suggestions for reforms need to balance supporting these actors and minimizing the influence of those who resist change.

A complicating factor with such reforms is that vested interests operate throughout societies and can be both public and private. For instance, in the case of fossil fuel companies, these can be both private companies and state-­owned companies. Since the burning of fossil fuels is the key driver of climate change, progressive climate action represents a significant threat to the fossil fuel industry. While they were for a long time engaged in denial campaigns, they have over time shifted to delaying tactics to prevent radical climate action (Green et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2023; Nasiritousi, 2017). States that rely on fossil fuels for jobs or revenues are likely to take their views into consideration and shape

their preferences and negotiation positions thereafter. Given the strong role of fossil fuels in the global economic system, it is no surprise that they exert strong influence in the international negotiations.

While the UNFCCC is a Party-­driven process, non-state actors have played important roles and their presence at UNFCCC meetings continues to grow (Nasiritousi, 2016). The greater involvement of business and other stakeholders is in many ways a strength of the UNFCCC. However, when these actors' interests do not align with the ultimate objectives of the UNFCCC and when conflicts of interest arise, the integrity and legitimacy of decision-­making within the UNFCCC come under question (see e.g., Bäckstrand et al., 2021; Dambacher et al., 2020). According to the Convention (UNFCCC, 1992, Article 7.6) and the admission procedures for observer organisations (UNFCCC, 2004), a private interest cannot be represented as an observer unless accredited through an admitted observer organisation, including business associations or other NGOs. Moreover, states can (and in many cases do) include actors from different sectors in their negotiation delegations. The Climate Investigation Center's mapping of fossil fuel company delegates in the US negotiation delegation in COP meetings between 1995 and 2018 (CIC, 2019) shows how common this type of participation is. According to the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, COP28 in Dubai granted access to a record number of fossil fuel lobbyists (Lakhani, 2023). Even though the exact influence of actors with a vested interest in preserving the status quo is difficult to trace, it is quite clear that they, in many cases, have had an impact on negotiated outcomes (Kinley et al., 2021; Kornek et al., 2020; Stoddard et al., 2021).
4 | TOWARDS ADDRESSING VESTED INTERESTS

UNFCCC reform is needed but calls to move the UNFCCC process to an implementation mode and tone down the need for high-­level negotiations are premature. There are several pressing issues that remain to be addressed in a multilateral setting to facilitate the implementation of the Paris Agreement. These include long-­standing issues such as adaptation, climate finance, and loss and damage, but also more recent issues such as phasing out fossil fuels and responsibility for carbon removals (Hermwille, 2021; Mohan et al., 2021; Naylor & Ford, 2023; van Asselt, 2021). COP28 in Dubai showcased this very clearly. The inclusion of calls for transitioning away from fossil fuels would not have been possible without high-­level political negotiations. For these discussions to take place in a conducive environment, reform proposals should drive change by focusing on procedures and practices that are in line with the objective of the UNFCCC. A key task will be to support interests that are aligned with achieving the Paris Agreement and lessening the influence of those interests that wish to obstruct change.

Such a task will likely require multiple approaches. In a recent study, Meckling and Nahm (2022) outline four strategies to overcome regulatory capture by vested interests: recruiting allies, limiting access, align-ing interests, and quieting interests. Some of these may be more feasible than others in an international setting. For instance, Dambacher et al. (2020) offer recommendations that seek to move towards a more transparent and inclusive UNFCCC process, while simultaneously addressing the potential risks that may arise from engagement with non-­state actors that hold interests diverging from those of the UNFCCC. They outline the need for conflict of interest rules to limit access of actors with interests that drive undesirable outcomes. This change should target not only the COP meetings but include the UNFCCC meetings outside of COPs. By developing such rules and defining what constitutes conflict of interest and undesirable outcomes, such interests could be weakened normatively and possibly even materially (Bäckstrand et al., 2021; Nasiritousi, 2017; Stoddard et al., 2021). Protests against the COP28 Presidency have focused on undue influence by oil and gas interests (Boycott COP28, 2023). While banning such influence is unforeseeable in the near future due to veto players (COP29 will be held in another petro-­state, namely Azerbaijan), incremental reforms towards such a goal that affect the normative and material interests of actors may be the most viable way forward. While time is running out for decisive decisions to hold temperatures within the Paris Agreement goals, a dynamic process towards weakening obstructionist and facilitating the inclusion of progressive interests is key to driving such discussions forward. What sets such efforts apart from other reform proposals is that it would strike at the heart of the challenge of addressing climate change and could potentially set off a norm-­cascade of anti-­fossil fuel norms (Green, 2018).

However, it is important to note that there may be trade-­offs between more ambitious outcomes made possible by restricting incumbent actors from access-ing the COPs, and a sense of responsibility to comply with agreements made possible by an inclusive process in which various interests have been listened to and have had a chance to influence the outcome (Bäckstrand et al., 2021). Thus, achieving an effective, inclusive, and just transition includes complex trade-­ offs and synergies (Pickering et al., 2022), which needs further exploration in relation to the representation of vested interests at COPs. A key question for future research is thus how to deal with vested interests while keeping the political process legitimate.

5 | FUTURE RESEARCH AGENDA

As the climate crisis heats up and countries increasingly turn to additional governance arrangements, such as carbon border adjustment mechanisms and the G7 climate club (Buylova et al., 2022; Nasiritousi & Reischl, 2022), multilateral fora such as the UNFCCC will remain key for maintaining legitimacy in global climate governance (Buylova et al., 2023; Tallberg et al., 2023). While the UNFCCC cannot on its own resolve all issues required for rapid climate transformation, it remains the only universal forum where crucial political climate discussions can be held. However, the UNFCCC will need to reform to stay relevant. Doing so calls for a new research agenda on dynamic institutional reform to reduce the influence of obstructive vested interests and to facilitate green spiralling in a politically legitimate manner. While the need for a more legitimate and effective UNFCCC is urgent, the multilateral process limits what can be expected in terms of outcomes. At the UNFCCC, where decision-­making takes place through consensus, incremental steps towards conflict of interest rules may be the most viable way forward. However, so far, such calls by NGOs have been blocked by countries that believe all voices should have a place at the table. Renewed efforts must push to weaken what has been called ‘fossil fuel diplomacy’ (Polychroniou, 2023).

While ultimately climate action depends on how states legislate and implement decisions, the UNFCCC has an important role in setting expectations and coordinating actions. By taking action against vested interests and setting off a green spiral, future decisions at the UNFCCC could be stronger which may create ripple effects. The green spiral could set off stronger actions domestically and weaken domestic vested interests through strengthened collective action for climate action and normative pressures, for example, through signals sent to investors. In other words, a more balanced representation of interests at the UNFCCC would increase the likelihood of achieving stronger outcomes at the UNFCCC, which in turn could stimulate more actions domestically for green spiralling. The suggested research agenda would thus examine conditions for strengthening and weakening specific types of interests which could in turn support creating enabling conditions for climate action at multiple levels and across organisations.

Future research could, for instance, cross-­fertilize scholarship on political economy and governance with literature on interest group politics (Zacher, 2023). A better understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the divestment movement may be one avenue for future research to understand how pressure can influence norms and material factors (Ayling & Gunningham, 2017). Research could, for example, examine questions such as how to move from an ‘all actors are needed at the table’ ideal to strengthening the voices of those whose goals align with the Paris Agreement. How can different vested interests be distinguished and what strategies are most effective in shifting influence from incumbent vested interests to new entrants and marginalised voices? Moreover, what monitoring and accountability mechanisms can be employed to support green spiralling? For instance, what criteria for participation is administratively and politically feasible to implement? We suggest that for a start there needs to be more transparency on who participates at the UNFCCC, potentially progress-ing over time to require participating organisations to have plans that address their climate impacts in line with agreed goals. The research agenda could also broaden the meaning of vested interests to include other factors that promote business as usual, including, for example, certain negotiation practices that hinder innovation and foster path dependency (see e.g., Buylova et al., 2023).

There is also a need to better understand how coalition building amongst states and non-­state actors could be used to drive change both inside and outside the UNFCCC process. Recent research has shown that lobbying success depends on how coalitions are formed and their characteristics (Junk, 2019). Different initiatives on the side of the UNFCCC are already underway to form coalitions to strengthen climate action (Bäckstrand et al., 2021; Nasiritousi & Reischl, 2022). A question that should be examined in the future is how to advance these green spiral initiatives in the UNFCCC and more widely. As countries implement their Nationally Determined Contributions to the Paris Agreement, new coalitions will emerge that could potentially be leveraged to break the stronghold of incumbent vested interests. Future research could also investigate what lessons that could be learned from national-­level politics and literatures on interest group campaigning, lobbying and democratic governance that would be feasible to apply at the international level.

The suggested research agenda would thus elaborate on the different dynamics that can drive policy ambition across governance levels and organisations. For the green spiral to be strengthened at the UNFCCC, greater strategic alignment and coordination with other multilateral bodies in fields such as finance, trade, energy, food, transport, and environment will be necessary. A research agenda that examines the enablers and blockers of such changes and how to address barriers to change could inform future reform proposals. This could help unlock action in other multilateral processes crucial for climate action, for example, at the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank, the World Trade Organisation, the International Energy

A research agenda that examines the dynamics of institutional reform across multilateral institutions could provide new insights into how to tackle grand challenges more effectively.

AUTHOR BIOGRAPHIES

Naghmeh Nasiritousi is a senior lecturer at Linköping University and a research fellow at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs, as well as the co-­director of the Centre for Climate Science and Policy Research, Linköping University. Her research focuses on global climate and energy governance, international institutions and issues of legitimacy and effectiveness.

Alexandra Buylova holds a PhD in Public Policy and is a research fellow at the Global Politics and Security Programme at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs. Her current research focuses on climate governance, more specifically examining national-­level decarbonisation strategies and policies, scrutinizing the role of state and non-­state actors in climate action, and the role of the UNFCCC in climate cooperation.

Mathias Fridahl is an Associate Professor at the Department of Thematic Studies, Linköping University, Sweden. He holds a PhD in Water and Environmental Studies on the topic of historical responsibility in the UNFCCC. His research focuses on climate policy and politics at multiple levels of governance, from subnational entities to universal multilateral forums.

Gunilla Reischl, PhD, Senior Research Fellow and Head of the Global Politics and Security Programme at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs. Her research focuses on global governance issues and international institutions, especially in the areas of environment and energy, climate security, and green transitions and democracy.
